title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation & its math
text: 🖼 Infographic 1 · RAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation & its math LLMs augmented with retrieved knowledge. Two pipelines: offline ingestion builds the index, online query retrieves, reranks and composes the prompt at runtime, so answers have fewer hallucinations and cite sources. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Retrieval playground Query: "How do we handle a P1 payments outage?" Adjust top-k and the rerank threshold to see what ends up in the prompt. Relevant chunks are marked ✓ so you can see recall vs. noise. top-k 5 Rerank min rerank score 0.50 3 chunks in prompt 3/3 relevant recalled 0 noise chunks ~203 context tokens Playbooks ✓ relevant P1 payments incident runbook: page on-call SRE within 5 min, open bridge, freeze deploys, notify payments lead. sim 0.89 rerank 0.95 IN PROMPT Past incident notes ✓ relevant 2026-03 payments outage: gateway timeouts from expired TLS cert; mitigation was failover to secondary PSP. sim 0.84 rerank 0.82 IN PROMPT Policies ✓ relevant Customer comms policy: outages over 30 min need a status-page update every 30 min. sim 0.81 rerank 0.77 IN PROMPT Product docs Payments API retry semantics and idempotency keys. sim 0.78 rerank 0.48 filtered Past incident notes 2025-11 email delivery outage caused by a DNS misconfiguration. sim 0.75 rerank 0.16 filtered Playbooks P2 minor degradation playbook: open a ticket, no paging required. sim 0.73 rerank 0.38 not retrieved Product docs Refund API: partial refunds and settlement timing. sim 0.69 rerank 0.11 not retrieved Policies On-call compensation and rotation policy. sim 0.66 rerank 0.07 not retrieved Sweet spot: retrieve broadly, then rerank and filter tightly. All relevant context goes in, with no noise. Design choices that matter Chunking Split on structure (headings, sections), not fixed characters. Keep metadata (source, date, ACL) on every chunk. Hybrid retrieval Combine vector similarity with keyword (BM25) search. Exact identifiers like error codes are often missed by embeddings alone. Rerank & filter A cross-encoder reranker over the top 20–50 candidates usually beats raising k. Filter by permissions before the LLM sees anything. Citations Give chunks IDs in the prompt and require the model to cite them. That makes answers auditable and lets you measure faithfulness. Evaluate Measure retrieval (recall@k, MRR) separately from generation (faithfulness, answer relevance). Fix the weaker half first. Freshness Incremental re-indexing on document change, plus TTLs for fast-moving sources such as incident notes. RAG formulas & concepts The math behind every RAG pipeline: embed, measure similarity, take the top-k, rerank, build context, generate, evaluate. Step through the pipeline, then try each formula on live numbers. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Embeddings & cosine similarity e = f emb ( text) · cos( q, d) = q · d ‖ q ‖ ‖ d ‖ Text becomes a vector that captures meaning. Cosine similarity compares direction, not length: 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated, −1 opposite. Real embeddings have hundreds to thousands of dimensions; this demo uses two. Drag the arrow tips on the right. q = [0.85, 0.45] d = [0.55, 0.75] q·d = 0.805 ‖q‖ = 0.962 ‖d‖ = 0.930 cos(q,d) = 0.900 angle 26° · very similar Chunking chunks ≈ ⌈ ( N − overlap) / ( size − overlap) ⌉ Document tokens 12,000 Chunk size 500 Overlap 100 +6 more 30 chunks → vectors to store 15,000 tokens embedded 25% extra from overlap Common approaches: fixed size (e.g. 500 tokens), with overlap (e.g. 100 tokens), or by structure (headings and sections). Overlap keeps sentences that straddle a boundary retrievable, at the cost of more vectors. Top-k retrieval & reranking D k = TopK d ∈ D sim( q, d) → s ′( q, d) = f rerank ( q, d) k 3 Apply reranker Final rank Chunk Initial score sim(q,d) Rerank score s′ 1 d₂ P1 escalation policy for payment failures 0.78 0.95 ▲ 1 2 d₁ Payments outage runbook: page on-call within 5 min 0.92 0.88 ▼ 1 3 d₄ Refund API reference 0.71 0.30 — – d₅ Past incident: PSP failover 0.55 not in top-3 – d₃ Office Wi-Fi setup guide 0.36 not in top-3 – d₆ Holiday calendar 0.30 not in top-3 The bi-encoder scores query and chunk separately, which is fast but coarse. The reranker reads them together, which is slower but sharper, and can reorder the list: watch d₂ overtake d₁. Context construction & generation Prompt to LLM Use the context below to answer the question. Cite chunk IDs. Context: [d₂] P1 escalation policy for payment failures [d₁] Payments outage runbook: page on-call within 5 min [d₄] Refund API reference Question: How do we handle a P1 payments outage? y = f LLM ( q, C), C = ( d 1, …, d k) The LLM generates the final answer from the query and the retrieved context, ideally citing the chunk IDs it used. Everything above decides what goes into C, and C caps the quality of y. Evaluation metrics Click a result to mark it relevant. Metrics update for the chosen k. k 5 Total relevant in the corpus: 5 (2 of them were never retrieved) #1 ✓ relevant #2 ✗ #3 ✓ relevant #4 ✗ #5 ✗ #6 ✓ relevant #7 ✗ #8 ✗ 0.40 Recall@5 = 2/5 0.40 Precision@5 = 2/5 1.00 MRR (first relevant at #1) Metric Formula What it measures Recall@k |relevant ∩ retrieved@k| / |relevant| How much of the relevant information was retrieved Precision@k |relevant ∩ retrieved@k| / k How many retrieved results are relevant MRR 1 / rank of first relevant How high the first good result appears Faithfulness LLM-judged Whether the answer is supported by the retrieved context Faithfulness does not guarantee factual correctness. Retrieved sources may themselves contain incorrect information. Key formulas Retrieval-augmented generation P ( y | q) ≈ Σ d ∈ top- k P ( d | q) · P ( y | q, d) The answer is generated conditioned on retrieved documents, weighted by how relevant each one is to the query (the original RAG formulation). Context budget T system + k · T chunk + T query + T answer ≤ T window More chunks means more recall but also more noise and cost. Check what fits, and what that costs per query. System tokens k chunks Tokens / chunk Answer tokens Window = 5,600 of 32,000 tokens (17.5%) ✓ fits Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: AI agents: the loop & its anatomy
h1: AI agents: the loop & its anatomy
text: 🖼 Infographic 2 · AI Agents AI agents: the loop & its anatomy An agent wraps an LLM in a loop: plan → act → observe → reflect, with memory and tools, until the goal is met or a stop condition fires. The result is closed-loop execution in real systems. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Human control ↔ autonomous action Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Move the slider to see which actions in the flight-booking example run on their own and which wait for a human. Autonomy level 2 · Approve external & irreversible Internal writes run automatically. Spending, messaging externally and deleting wait for approval. Search flights read Auto Read calendar & preferences read Auto Add calendar event internal write Auto Book ticket ($640) spend money Needs approval Email confirmation to traveler external message Needs approval Cancel an existing booking destructive Needs approval Whatever the level, put a fail-closed risk gate in front of irreversible actions (payments, deletes, external messages) and log every tool call for audit and evals. Agent building blocks Planner Breaks the goal into steps (ReAct, plan-and-execute, tree search). Re-plans when observations contradict the plan. Memory Short-term memory is the conversation and scratchpad. Long-term memory holds user preferences and past outcomes, read and written by the agent. Tools Typed functions with clear schemas: ticketing, email, data tools. Read tools are cheap; write tools need guardrails. Stop conditions Goal satisfied, step or token budget exhausted, repeated failure, or human interrupt. Without them, agents loop. The anatomy of an AI agent Every agent is the same four parts. A brain (the LLM) runs a loop: perceive, reason, act, observe. Memory supplies context, short-term in the window and long-term in a store. Tools turn the model's function calls into real actions. Guardrails check every action before it runs. The loop ends with a final answer, or when it hits its iteration or budget limit. Brain, memory, tools and guardrails around one loop. Press Play. Run the agent loop Step through a real-looking task. Watch the context window fill and get compacted, tool calls pass through the policy gate, one action get rejected, and the loop stop. Change the limits, or switch the guardrails off, to see what changes. Task: Find last quarter's refund total and email a summary to the finance team. Context window Max iterations Token budget Guardrails on Context window 2,200 / 8,000 Tokens spent 0 / 60,000 Next iteration › Run to the end Reset Iteration 0 · compactions 0 # Reason Act Gate valid · scope · budget Observe Press "Next iteration" to start the loop. The four parts 🧠 Memory Short-term: the context window holds the instructions, the conversation and recent tool results. It fills up fast. Compaction: when it's nearly full, older turns are summarized so the agent keeps the gist and frees room. Long-term: a vector store, knowledge base or files. The agent retrieves the top-k relevant items and writes back what it learns. 🔧 Tools The model emits a function call: a name and JSON arguments. The runtime dispatches it to the right tool (search, code, files, APIs, MCP servers) and executes it. The result comes back as an observation in the next turn's context. 🔁 The loop Perceive the task and context, reason and plan, act by calling a tool, observe the result, reflect, repeat. Stop when there's a final answer (a turn with no tool call), at max iterations, or when the token, time or cost budget runs out. 🛡 Guardrails Validate: is the call well-formed and its arguments safe? Scope: is this tool and this target allowed for this user and task? Budget: are there iterations, tokens, money and rate left? Any failure rejects the action; the agent sees why and adapts. The gate fails closed. Related: AI agents · Tool call anatomy · AI guardrails · Orchestrators & specialized agents · Risk Kernel Key formulas: The anatomy of an AI agent Cost of the loop tokens ≈ Σ t =1 T C t, C t = C 0 + t·Δ Every iteration re-reads the whole context, which grows with each tool result. Cost grows roughly with the square of the number of iterations, which is why compaction and max-iteration limits matter. Starting context Added per iteration Iterations = ≈ 96,000 input tokens When to compact compact when C t ≥ θ · W Trigger compaction at a share θ of the window W, leaving room for the next tool result and the answer. Window (tokens) Threshold θ Largest expected tool result = compact at 160,000 tokens · headroom 40,000 ✓ fits the largest result The SPAR framework S ense → P lan → A ct → R eflect: how an AI agent goes from perceiving its environment to taking an action and improving over time. Follow a research agent through all four stages. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. The four stages Stage What it is Typical mechanisms Research agent example S · Sense How the agent perceives and understands its environment Documents, user interface, web search, vector DB, knowledge graph Go through the company DB and the internet to gather facts P · Plan The reasoning stage: decide how best to achieve the goal CoT, ToT, GoT, ReAct, Reflexion, Plan-and-Execute Use CoT to break the workflow into simple research tasks A · Act Execute the strategy with digital tools or platforms Computer use, generate docs, call APIs, generate visuals, update DB, schedule tasks Build an entire PPT from the research output R · Reflect Evaluate outcomes and improve logic or strategy over time LLM feedback, user feedback, revise plan, update tool calls, update logs Update the draft based on user feedback Planning strategies at a glance CoT · Chain of Thought Reason step by step in one linear chain. Cheap and good for decomposition. ToT · Tree of Thought Branch into alternatives, evaluate them, prune. Good for search-like problems. GoT · Graph of Thought Thoughts as a graph that can merge and reuse partial results. ReAct Interleave reasoning with tool actions and observations. The default for tool-using agents. Reflexion Self-critique after attempts, with the lessons stored in memory for the next try. P&E · Plan-and-Execute Write the full plan first, then execute the steps, often with a cheaper executor model. Key formulas: The SPAR framework ReAct trajectory τ = ( thought 1, act 1, obs 1, …, thought T), cost = T ·( c think + c tool) Sense → plan → act → reflect repeats T times. Cost and latency scale linearly with the number of cycles. Cycles T Tokens per thought $ / 1M tokens Tool $ per call = ≈ $0.0300 per task Tree of Thought search size nodes = Σ l =0 D b l Branching b thoughts at depth D explodes quickly. Pruning keeps only the best few per level. Branching b Depth D = 40 thoughts to evaluate without pruning Key formulas Compounding reliability P (success) = Π i =1 n p i ≈ p n Even very reliable steps compound badly over long chains. That's why agents need verification, retries and short plans. Per-step success Steps = 59.9% chance the whole run succeeds With a retry per step p step = 1 − (1 − p) r +1 Retries (with verification that detects the failure) lift each step's success rate and therefore the whole chain's. Per-attempt success Retries Steps = step 99% → whole run 90.4% Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: Model Context Protocol & server roles
text: 🖼 Infographic 3 · MCP ✓ Last reviewed Nov 23, 2026 Model Context Protocol & server roles A standard way for LLM applications to use tools and data. Hosts (an IDE, a desktop assistant, an internal playground) run MCP clients that talk to MCP servers, which wrap real systems like a CRM, a SQL warehouse or a file drive. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Why a standard: M × N → M + N AI apps / hosts (M) 5 Tools & data sources (N) 12 Custom integrations without MCP (M × N) 60 With MCP: one client per host, one server per tool (M + N) 17 The primitives Servers expose Tools model-controlled Functions the model can call, e.g. run_query, create_ticket, described with JSON Schema. Resources app-controlled Read-only context addressed by URI, e.g. file:///guide.md, DB rows. Prompts user-controlled Reusable templates and workflows the user can invoke. Clients offer Sampling The server asks the host's LLM to generate something, so the server needs no model keys of its own. Roots Which folders or URIs the server is allowed to work within. Elicitation The server asks the user for missing input mid-task. Transport: JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio (local servers) or Streamable HTTP (remote servers, with OAuth for authorization). The 7 architectural roles of an MCP server Not all MCP servers are the same. Choosing the right role keeps servers purpose-built, composable, secure by design and production-ready. Pick a role to see its flow. 01 Tool Lean-in 02 Context Provider 03 Gateway Connector 04 Stateful Session Manager 05 Sandboxed Executor 06 Workflow Packager 07 Delegated Reasoner Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. 01 · Tool Lean-in One-to-one transport One service per MCP server. Simple, debuggable and easy to version. Example: GitHub MCP Use when You wrap a single API and want clean ownership and versioning. Watch out Many small servers mean tool sprawl. Pair with a gateway as you scale. Purpose-built Each role solves one problem better. Composable Combine roles into powerful agent systems. Secure by design Isolation, auth and state management where they matter. Production-ready From simple tools to complex enterprise workflows. Composing roles Real deployments combine roles. A typical enterprise setup has a Gateway Connector in front of several Tool Lean-in servers, which centralizes auth, rate limits and logging. Context Providers feed RAG-style reads. A Sandboxed Executor is the trust boundary for code. Workflow Packagers expose approved runbooks so the agent can't improvise risky steps. Key formulas: The 7 architectural roles of an MCP server Gateway rate limit (token bucket) tokens( t) = min( B, tokens( t −Δ) + r ·Δ) A bucket of size B refills at rate r. Bursts up to B pass; sustained traffic is capped at r per second. Bucket B Refill r / s Burst size = 100 pass immediately; the rest wait ≈ 15 s Community MCP servers worth a look Each server below gives an agent one new skill. All are open source, published in October or November 2026, and young: treat them as experiments, not infrastructure. Skill Server What it adds Licence Check first See browse · anomalyco The agent uses your real browser, through a Chromium extension MIT It acts in your signed-in sessions. Use a separate browser profile; read the install script before piping it to a shell Touch Pinky · DIYgod The agent operates your iPhone or Android phone, with you in the loop Apache-2.0 Phone access is broad. Approve each action and keep payment apps out of reach Remember whatsapp-mcp · finereli Searches your own WhatsApp chats, read-only MIT Your messages, and other people's, go to the model. A hosted version exists; self-host for anything sensitive Plan Kanzo · emanuele-em One self-hosted kanban board shared by you and your agents AGPL-3.0 AGPL: modifying it and offering it as a service means sharing your changes Spot new-term-radar · zhuyansen A daily radar for new AI model, product and repo names MIT Depends on scraping public sites; expect it to break when they change Study reverse-engineer-marketing · dansugc Paste a link, get the site's ads, SEO, social and funnel, with evidence MIT Use it on public information only and respect each site's terms Hear audio-studio-mcp · kanaworksai-hue Songs, background music and sound effects made locally MIT Needs an Apple Silicon Mac or an NVIDIA GPU. Check each model's licence before commercial use Make Kokon · GabrieleLozupone Edit photos by describing the change, on your own GPU AGPL-3.0 A large local model download; AGPL applies as for Kanzo Before installing any MCP server: read its code or install script, run it with the fewest permissions and no production credentials, pin a version instead of tracking the latest, and check what data leaves your machine. A server's tool descriptions go straight into the model's context, so a malicious one can steer the agent. See attacks on agent tools & MCP. From a community round-up ("8 free MCP servers"). Repositories, owners and licences were checked on GitHub on 27 Nov 2026; the "Check first" notes are this site's. Governance MCP is an open standard. Anthropic donated it to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), a Linux Foundation project formed in December 2025 that also hosts A2A, AGENTS.md and goose. The spec ships in dated versions (the latest is 2026-07-28) under a formal deprecation policy with at least twelve months' notice. See what changed in the 2026-07-28 spec. Key formulas Integrations: M × N → M + N without MCP: M · N with MCP: M + N One client per host and one server per tool replaces a custom integration for every pair (see the calculator above). Availability of a multi-server call A = Π i A i If a task needs several servers in series, their availabilities multiply. Per-server availability Servers needed = 98% (≈ 858 min down / month) Sources & review Time-sensitive · last reviewed Nov 23, 2026 Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: A2A
text: 🖼 Infographic 4 · A2A ✓ Last reviewed Nov 23, 2026 Agent-to-Agent coordination MCP connects an agent to tools. A2A connects an agent to other agents, which may be owned by other teams, partners or vendors. Agents publish Agent Cards, get discovered through a registry, and exchange tasks, status events and artifacts through a governed gateway. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Task lifecycle Lights up as you step through the flow above. submitted → working → input-required → completed terminal: failed → canceled MCP vs A2A MCP A2A Connects Agent ↔ tools, data, prompts Agent ↔ agent Other side is Deterministic capability (function, resource) Opaque, autonomous peer with its own tools and reasoning Unit of work Tool call → result Task with lifecycle → messages, status, artifacts Discovery tools/list, resources/list Agent Card (skills, endpoint, auth) via registry Duration Usually short, synchronous Can run long, stream updates, pause for input Use together An agent uses MCP for its own tools and A2A to delegate to agents it doesn't own. Version & governance Stable v1.0 A2A reached v1.0, its first stable, production-ready release, in March 2026. Build against 1.x and check the spec's changelog before relying on newer features. Neutral home Agentic AI Foundation Google donated A2A to the Linux Foundation in June 2025. In August 2026 it moved into the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), the Linux Foundation's home for agent standards, alongside MCP and AGENTS.md. More than 150 organizations backed it at its first anniversary. Sources: Google Open Source Blog, Linux Foundation, AAIF. Key formulas Delegation chain P = Π i p i, L = Σ i L i Every hop to another agent multiplies the risk of failure and adds latency. Keep chains short and make every hop auditable. Per-agent success Hops Seconds per hop = 91.3% success · ≈ 12 s Sources & review Time-sensitive · last reviewed Nov 23, 2026 Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: Harness, loop & graph engineering
text: 🖼 Infographic 5 · Building agent systems Harness, loop & graph engineering Three ways to build agent systems: a harness to empower one agent, a loop to refine output, a graph to handle complex work. Most production systems nest them, for example a graph whose nodes are harnessed agents with internal loops. Agent Harness Engineering Loop Engineering Graph Engineering Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Agent Harness Loop Graph Idea Give an agent the right tools, guardrails and context to operate safely and effectively. Design iterative workflows where the agent loops until the goal is achieved. Orchestrate multiple agents and tools as a graph of interconnected nodes. Purpose Empower a single agent to do the job end-to-end. Refine, iterate and improve until done. Solve complex problems through collaboration and specialization. Best for Well-defined tasks that one agent with the right capabilities can handle. Tasks that need iteration, refinement or feedback loops. Complex, multi-step problems that need specialization and coordination. Strengths Simple to build and maintain Clear boundaries Reliable and predictable Improves quality over time Self-correcting Works well with evaluation loops Highly scalable Modular and flexible Resilient and distributed Limitations Single point of failure Harder to scale complexity Limited by one agent's context window Can loop infinitely Needs good stop conditions Slower for complex tasks More complex to design Harder to debug Higher orchestration overhead Example A research agent that can search, analyze and write a full report. A content-writer agent that drafts, reviews and improves until it meets the standard. A customer support system with retrieval, verification, escalation and follow-up agents. Key takeaway Harness for empowerment. Loop for refinement. Graph for complexity. Choose the approach that fits the problem. Loop simulator An evaluator–optimizer loop: draft, score, refine. Set the quality bar and the iteration budget. A good stop condition is the difference between self-correction and an infinite loop. Quality bar 85 Max iterations 6 First-draft quality 50 Run loop bar 85 50 63 74 84 89 Stopped: quality bar met after 5 iterations. Gains shrink each round, which is typical of refinement loops. Which pattern fits? One agent with the right tools could do it end-to-end Fits in one context window, and one set of permissions is enough. Quality improves with critique and revision There is a measurable bar, such as tests, a rubric or an evaluator. Subtasks need different specialists, permissions or owners For example retrieval, verification, escalation and follow-up. → Agent harness One well-equipped agent is the simplest reliable option. Invest in tools, context and guardrails before adding more agents. Harness engineering: from powerful models to reliable results A harness is the control system around a model: guides that raise the odds of a good first attempt, sensors that let the agent see and correct what it did, and state that lets work survive the end of a context window. The same model can produce broken or working software depending on what surrounds it. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. The seven load-bearing concepts Tick the ones your agent already has. 1 · Closed-loop verification Let the model see, check and correct its work. Result: Fewer errors, higher reliability 2 · Context budgeting Use context intentionally; reset and summarize. Result: Longer, cheaper runs 3 · Externalized state Keep progress outside the context window (files, git). Result: Work survives across sessions 4 · Verifiable increments Ship small, testable steps with clear acceptance tests. Result: Steady progress, less rework 5 · Independent evaluation External judges, tests or humans; never let a model grade its own work against a number it can move. Result: Trustworthy measurements 6 · Action-space design Give the model a small, well-chosen set of tools. Result: Fewer mistakes, better outcomes 7 · Trace-driven steering loop Use logs, traces and metrics to improve, and delete components as models advance. Result: A simpler, stronger harness over time 0/7 load-bearing concepts in place. Next to add: Closed-loop verification. Real-world evidence: same model, different harness Anthropic · retro game maker A solo agent ran about 20 min for about $9, and the game didn't respond to input. A planner–generator–evaluator harness ran about 6 hours for about $200, and the game played successfully. LangChain · Terminal Bench 2.0 Before 52.8 After 66.5 Same model; only the system prompt, tools and middleware changed. Vercel · internal data agent They removed about 80% of the tools. The success rate went from 80% to 100% on a small internal question set, with fewer steps and fewer tokens. As reported in the infographic, which rates its own confidence as medium for each case. Use them as directional, not as benchmarks. The Anthropic case is set out in full below. Three agents around one prompt Asked to grade their own work, agents confidently praise it, even when the quality is obviously mediocre. Anthropic's Labs team fixed this by separating the jobs: a planner writes the spec, a generator builds it a piece at a time, and an evaluator uses the running app like a user would and fails anything below the bar. Walk the loop. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Agent Planner Expands a 1–4 sentence prompt into a product spec: features, user stories, design. It stays at product level and leaves implementation to the generator. In the game run, one sentence became 16 features across ten sprints. File Sprint contract Before any code is written, the generator and the evaluator agree what "done" means for the next piece of work and how it will be tested. The spec stays high level; the contract makes it testable. Agent Generator Builds one feature at a time against the contract, commits with git, checks its own work, then hands off to QA. It never signs off on its own work. Agent Evaluator Clicks through the running app with Playwright (through an MCP server), testing the UI, the API and the database. It files every bug against the contract. One sprint alone had 27 criteria. Rule Hard thresholds Each sprint is graded on product depth, functionality, visual design and code quality. A score below the bar on any one fails the sprint, and detailed feedback goes back to the generator. Lesson Simplify as models improve Every part of a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do alone. With a stronger model, the team dropped sprints entirely and the generator built for over two hours in one go. Re-test each part when the model changes. Run Time Cost Result Solo agent, one-sentence prompt for a retro game maker 20 min $9 Looked plausible; the game didn't respond to input Three-agent harness, same prompt (sprints, Opus 4.5) 6 hr $200 Playable game with far more features; the evaluator still missed some deeper bugs Simplified harness, no sprints (Opus 4.6), a different prompt: an audio workstation in the browser 3 hr 50 min $124.70 Working app; QA still caught real gaps in the first round The harness costs far more than a solo run; it's worth it when a broken result costs more than the tokens. The third run built a different app, so don't read it as the same job done cheaper. Source: Anthropic, Harness design for long-running application development (March 2026). A prompt that sets up the same loop in a coding agent such as Claude Code. Fill in the three braces; the rest runs as written. THREE-AGENT HARNESS {APP IN 1-4 SENTENCES} · {STACK} · {QUALITY BAR} 01 PLANNER Expand {APP} into a product spec: features, user stories, design. Stay at product level, no implementation details. Split into sprints. 02 CONTRACT Before each sprint, write contract.md: what gets built, how it is tested. The evaluator reviews it. Iterate until both agree on "done". 03 GENERATOR Build one feature per sprint against the contract. Commit with git. Self-check, then hand off to QA. Never sign off on your own work. 04 EVALUATOR Click through the running app with Playwright, like a user would. Test the UI, the API and the database. File every bug with file:line. 05 THRESHOLDS Grade product depth, functionality, visual design, code quality. Any score under {QUALITY BAR} fails the sprint. Feedback goes back. 06 LOOP Fail, fix, retest. Update progress.md after every sprint. Stop when every feature in the spec passes. Report cost and time. Build the loop first, the evaluator second, orchestration last. Keep state outside the model, keep the action space small, and remove harness components as models improve. Related: harness vs loop vs graph, Claude Code dev kit. Key formulas: Harness engineering: from powerful models to reliable results pass@k pass@ k = 1 − C( n − c, k) C( n, k) ≈ 1 − (1 − p) k The chance at least one of k attempts passes, given c of n samples passed. Independent evaluation (tests, judges) is what makes the retries worthwhile. Single-attempt pass rate Attempts k = pass@5 ≈ 88.4% Key formulas Iterations to reach the quality bar n = ⌈ ln( (1 − bar) / (1 − q 0)) ln(1 − α) ⌉ With a fixed fraction α of the gap closed per loop, this is how many loops it takes. Set the max-iterations cap above it. First draft q₀ Bar α = 4 iterations Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: LLM optimization & serving
text: 🖼 Infographic 6 · Performance LLM optimization & serving The goal: make LLMs smaller, faster, cheaper and more efficient without sacrificing quality. Techniques act at different stages: training, compression, inference and serving. Filter by stage and click a card for trade-offs. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. All Fine-tuning Knowledge Compression Inference Architecture 1. PEFT Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Fine-tune only small parts of the model (adapters, prefixes, low-rank updates) instead of the full model. Fine-tuning ↓ cost ↓ memory Benefit: Lower cost, less memory, faster training. One base model can serve many task adapters. Trade-off: Can trail full fine-tuning on tasks far from the base model's training data. 2. LoRA Low-Rank Adaptation Adds lightweight trainable matrices A (d×r) and B (r×d). The weight update BA has rank r, much smaller than d. Fine-tuning ↓ cost ↓ memory Benefit: Efficient fine-tuning, often with under 1% trainable params. Adapters can be merged into the weights, adding no latency. Trade-off: Rank and target-module choices matter. Too low a rank underfits. Open calculator ↓ 3. QLoRA Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation Freezes the base model in 4-bit and trains LoRA adapters on top in higher precision. Fine-tuning ↓ memory ↓ cost Benefit: Even lower memory use with high performance. Large models can be fine-tuned on a single GPU. Trade-off: Slower steps because of de-quantization, and a small quality gap in some cases. 4. RAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation Fetches external knowledge dynamically instead of retraining the model. Knowledge ↑ quality ↑ freshness Benefit: More accurate, up-to-date and context-aware answers, with citations. Trade-off: Quality is capped by retrieval quality, and it adds latency and tokens. See the interactive RAG flow → 5. Quantization 16-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit Reduces the numeric precision of weights (and sometimes activations or KV cache) to cut memory and improve speed. Compression ↓ memory ↓ latency ↓ cost Benefit: Smaller model size and faster inference, often 2–4× less memory. Trade-off: Accuracy can drop at 4-bit and below. Needs good calibration methods (GPTQ, AWQ and others). Open calculator ↓ 6. Distillation Knowledge Distillation Trains a smaller "student" model using a larger "teacher" model's outputs. Compression ↓ latency ↓ cost Benefit: Faster, smaller models that keep good performance on target tasks. Trade-off: Needs teacher compute and data, and the student rarely beats the teacher. 7. Pruning Remove weights / neurons Removes unnecessary weights, heads or layers to make models smaller and faster, usually followed by brief retraining. Compression ↓ memory ↓ latency Benefit: Reduced model size and faster inference. Trade-off: Unstructured sparsity only speeds things up on kernels and hardware that exploit it. 8. Flash Attention IO-aware exact attention An optimized attention kernel that works in tiles in fast on-chip memory and never builds the full N×N matrix. Inference ↓ latency ↓ memory Benefit: Higher throughput and lower memory use with identical results. Enables long contexts. Trade-off: GPU-specific kernels, and the gains depend on hardware generation. 9. KV Cache Key-Value Cache Reuses previously computed attention keys and values so each new token doesn't recompute the whole prefix. Inference ↓ latency Benefit: Faster generation and lower compute cost. Trade-off: Memory grows with sequence length × batch size, and is often the real serving bottleneck. Open calculator ↓ 10. MoE Mixture of Experts A router activates only a few expert sub-networks per token instead of the entire model. Architecture ↓ cost ↑ quality Benefit: Higher efficiency and scalability with fewer active parameters. Trade-off: All experts must still fit in memory, and routing and load balancing add complexity. Bonus: more optimization areas Prompt optimization Better prompts mean better outputs at lower cost. Context window management Trim, summarize or chunk long inputs. Batching Process multiple requests together for efficiency (continuous batching). Speculative decoding A small draft model proposes tokens and the large model verifies several at once. Hardware optimization GPUs, TPUs, optimized kernels and efficient serving. Model serving & caching Optimize serving, prefix and semantic caching, and load balancing. Back-of-envelope calculators Quantization memory LoRA trainable params KV cache size Model size (B params) Presets FP32 280 GB FP16 / BF16 140 GB INT8 / FP8 70 GB INT4 / NF4 35 GB Weights only: params × bits ÷ 8. A 70B model drops from 140 GB at 16-bit to 35 GB at 4-bit, which fits a single 80 GB GPU. Estimates for weights or cache only. Real deployments add activations, framework overhead and fragmentation, often 10–30% more. ✓ Last reviewed Nov 20, 2026 LLM serving & hardware Serving an LLM is a memory problem as much as a compute problem. Prefill (reading the prompt) is compute-bound; decode (generating tokens) is bound by memory bandwidth. Serving engines squeeze GPUs with continuous batching, paged KV caches, fused attention kernels and prompt caching. Walk a request through an engine. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. The techniques Prompt caching Don't re-read the same prefix When many requests share a long prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, a document), the engine stores its processed KV state and reuses it. Providers usually bill cache hits at a fraction of the normal input price and cut time to first token. Keep the stable part first and byte-identical; put anything that varies after it. Continuous batching Fill every GPU slot Static batching waits for the slowest request in the batch. Continuous (in-flight) batching adds new requests and removes finished ones at every decode step, raising throughput several-fold with little latency cost. Standard in vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and SGLang. FlashAttention Attention without the memory traffic Computes attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip SRAM instead of writing the full n×n matrix to GPU memory. Same result, much faster and far less memory, which is what made long contexts practical. PagedAttention Virtual memory for the KV cache Stores each sequence's KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like OS pages, instead of one contiguous reservation. Almost no wasted memory, more concurrent requests, and shared blocks for common prefixes. Prefill/decode split Different jobs, different hardware Large deployments run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools (disaggregated serving) and use chunked prefill so long prompts don't stall everyone's token stream. Speculative & quantized Fewer bytes, more tokens Quantized weights (8-bit, 4-bit) mean fewer bytes per token; speculative decoding produces several tokens per big-model pass. See LLM optimization. Accelerators Hardware Strength Typical role Data-center GPUs (NVIDIA H/B-class, AMD MI-class) High-bandwidth memory (HBM), fast interconnect, mature software (CUDA, ROCm) Training and most inference TPUs (Google) Matrix units and pod-scale interconnect Training and serving on Google Cloud Inference ASICs (Trainium/Inferentia, Groq, Cerebras and others) Cost or latency optimized for serving High-volume or ultra-low-latency inference NPUs in phones and laptops Low power, always available On-device assistants, transcription, vision Rule of thumb: model weights + KV cache must fit in accelerator memory, and decode speed is roughly memory bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token. Use the calculators below. Edge & on-device AI Why on-device Privacy (data never leaves the device), offline use, no per-token cost, and instant response for small tasks. How Small models (1–8B parameters) quantized to 4 bits, run through runtimes such as llama.cpp, Core ML, ONNX Runtime or vendor NPU SDKs. Hybrid pattern Handle simple requests on the device and escalate hard ones to the cloud, with the user's consent and clear disclosure. Key formulas: LLM serving & hardware Does it fit in GPU memory? M ≈ P · b 8 + KV + overhead Weights in bytes plus the KV cache for all concurrent sequences, plus roughly 10–20% overhead. Parameters (billions) Bits per weight KV cache (GB) GPU memory (GB) GPUs = ≈ 103 GB needed vs 160 GB available → fits Decode speed bound tokens/s ≲ memory bandwidth bytes read per token Each decode step reads all weights once, so bandwidth caps single-stream speed. Batching shares that read across users. Memory bandwidth (TB/s) Parameters (billions) Bits per weight = ≈ 47 tokens/s per stream (upper bound) Prompt caching savings savings = h · T prefix · (1 − r) · p 10 6 · calls h is the cache hit rate and r the cached price as a fraction of the normal input price. Shared prefix tokens Hit rate Cached price fraction $ per 1M input Calls per day = ≈ $275 saved per day Key formulas Weights memory M = P · b 8 bytes Parameters × bits ÷ 8 (see the quantization calculator above). LoRA trainable parameters Δ W = B A, params = L · m ·2· d · r Low-rank update with rank r ≪ d (see the LoRA calculator above). KV cache size KV = 2 · L · h kv · d h · b · s · n Grows with context length s and concurrency n (see the KV calculator above). Speculative decoding speedup speedup = 1 − α γ+1 (1 − α)(γ· c + 1) A draft model proposes γ tokens. α is the acceptance rate and c the draft model's cost relative to the main model. Acceptance α Draft tokens γ Draft cost ratio c = ≈ 2.8× faster Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: RAG architectures
h1: 10 RAG architectures, from naive to multi-agent
text: 🖼 Infographic 1b · RAG architectures 10 RAG architectures, from naive to multi-agent Every variant fixes a specific weakness of the one before it: bad ranking, short queries, wrong documents, missing relationships, unnecessary retrieval, or a single fixed source. Pick a variant to walk through its flow. 1 Naive RAG 2 Retrieve-and-rerank 3 Multimodal RAG 4 HyDE 5 Corrective RAG 6 Graph RAG 7 Hybrid RAG 8 Adaptive RAG 9 Agentic RAG (router) 10 Multi-agent RAG Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. 1 · Naive RAG Embed → search → put the results in the prompt. Best for Prototypes, small clean corpora, FAQ bots cost: Lowest Watch out Irrelevant chunks, and no recovery when retrieval misses. Compare them all # Architecture Core idea Best for Cost Watch out 1 Naive RAG Embed → search → put the results in the prompt. Prototypes, small clean corpora, FAQ bots Lowest Irrelevant chunks, and no recovery when retrieval misses. 2 Retrieve-and-rerank Retrieve wide (top-50), then a cross-encoder picks the best few. Most production RAG. The best quality gain per unit of effort. Low (+50–200 ms) The reranker adds latency, so cap the candidate count. 3 Multimodal RAG Index images, tables, audio and video alongside text in a shared embedding space. Manuals with diagrams, slide decks, product photos, scanned forms Medium–high Embedding cost and storage. Captions alone lose detail, so keep the originals. 4 HyDE The LLM writes a hypothetical answer first. Search with that, not with the short question. Short or vague queries, and a vocabulary gap between users and docs +1 LLM call A hallucinated draft can steer retrieval wrong. The final answer must still come from real docs. 5 Corrective RAG Grade what was retrieved. If it's weak, fall back to web search and refine. Open-domain questions, and knowledge bases with coverage gaps Medium Web results need trust filtering. The grader threshold needs tuning. 6 Graph RAG An LLM extracts entities and relations into a knowledge graph. Retrieval walks the graph as well as vectors. Multi-hop questions ("which services depend on X?"), global summaries High indexing cost Graph build is expensive and can drift. Entity resolution is hard. 7 Hybrid RAG Run dense vectors, keyword (BM25) and graph retrieval in parallel, then fuse the results. Enterprise search with exact IDs, error codes, names and semantics together Medium Fusion weights need tuning. More indexes to keep in sync. 8 Adaptive RAG Classify the query first: skip retrieval, or pick the right retrieval strategy. Mixed traffic, from chit-chat and simple facts to deep research Saves cost on easy queries A misclassified query takes the wrong path, so log and evaluate the router. 9 Agentic RAG (router) An agent decides which source or tool to query, checks whether the context is enough, and re-queries if not. Questions spanning docs, live data and the web Medium–high (multiple LLM calls) Loops and latency. Set a step budget. 10 Multi-agent RAG An orchestrator delegates to specialist retrieval agents, each with its own tools, then synthesizes. Research-grade questions across many systems (docs, web, Slack, Gmail) Highest Orchestration overhead, duplicated work and harder tracing. Rule of thumb: start with retrieve-and-rerank + hybrid search. Add corrective or adaptive routing when you see failures. Reach for graph or agentic RAG only when questions are multi-hop or span several systems. RAG vs Agentic RAG vs Graph RAG Different approaches, same goal: better answers. RAG = retrieve. Agentic RAG = plan + act. Graph RAG = think in connections. Switch between them to compare the flows. RAG · retrieve and generate Agentic RAG · plan, act, generate Graph RAG · knowledge graph + retrieval Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Side by side RAG Agentic RAG Graph RAG Core loop Retrieve → augment → generate Plan → retrieve with tools → evaluate → generate Classify → local graph traversal or global community summaries → synthesize Knowledge store Vector DB (index + metadata) Vector DB plus tools, APIs and MCP servers Vector DB plus knowledge graph plus community reports (offline indexed) Decides to retrieve? Always Planning agent decides; evaluator can re-retrieve Always, but chooses local vs global search Strengths Simple and effective · factual Q&A · single-turn tasks Planning and tool integration · multi-step reasoning · complex tasks Complex, multi-entity queries · "big picture" questions · more contextual answers Cost / latency Lowest Medium–high (several LLM calls) High indexing cost; global search is many map calls Fails when The answer spans many documents or needs a decision Loops without a step budget; evaluator is mis-tuned Graph extraction is noisy; data changes faster than re-indexing Key formulas: RAG vs Agentic RAG vs Graph RAG Graph RAG global search: LLM calls calls = ⌈ C B ⌉ + 1 Global search maps over every community report in batches of B, then makes one final reduce call. That's why it costs far more than local search. Community reports Reports per batch = 13 LLM calls per global query Agentic RAG expected cost E[calls] = 1 + p retrieve ·( s + 1 + r) A planner call, then for queries that need retrieval: s sub-queries, an evaluator, and r expected re-retrievals. Share needing retrieval Sub-queries Expected re-retrievals = ≈ 4.08 model/tool calls per query Key formulas Reciprocal rank fusion (Hybrid RAG) RRF( d) = Σ r ∈ retrievers 1 k + rank r ( d) Merge ranked lists from vector, keyword and graph search without calibrating their scores. k ≈ 60 is the usual constant. Rank in vector list Rank in BM25 list Rank in graph list k = RRF = 0.04815 BM25 keyword score BM25 = Σ t ∈ q IDF( t)· tf·( k 1 +1) tf + k 1 ·(1 − b + b · | d | avgdl) Exact-term matching that rewards rare words and dampens repeated terms. It catches IDs and codes that embeddings blur (k₁ ≈ 1.2, b ≈ 0.75). HyDE query vector e q = 1 N Σ j f emb ( h j), h j ~ LLM( q) Embed one or more hypothetical answers (optionally averaged with the query) instead of the short question. title: MCP protocol & clients
text: 🖼 Infographic 3b · MCP architecture ✓ Last reviewed Nov 21, 2026 MCP protocol & clients The standardized bridge between AI models and external systems. MCP decouples AI from systems: change servers, not your agent. Below is the message flow between the AI application, the MCP client, the MCP server and the external system. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Layers Application AI apps, agents and tools that use MCP. They request context, invoke tools and consume results. Client Lives in the host and handles discovery, requests and responses, one per server connection. Protocol / transport Standard message format (JSON-RPC 2.0), security, reliability. Server Exposes capabilities (tools, resources, prompts) in a standardized way. Resource Databases, APIs, files, cloud, SaaS apps, IoT devices: the real systems behind the server. Example: file system server Click a capability to see the JSON-RPC exchange and the governance it needs. list_files() read_file() write_file() search_files() delete_file() → Request client → server { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 8, "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "read_file", "arguments": { "path": "/workspace/README.md" } } } ← Response server → client { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 8, "result": { "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "# Payments Service\nRun `npm test` before…" } ] } } read Safe read, but watch for secrets (.env) and keep reads inside roots. Protocol highlights Transport JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio for local servers and Streamable HTTP for remote ones (stateless since 2026-07-28, so any instance behind a load balancer can answer). HTTP+SSE is deprecated; WebSocket would be a custom transport. Message format Structured JSON requests, responses and notifications. Tool inputs are described with JSON Schema, and outputs can be structured. Security OAuth 2.1 authorization for HTTP servers, with Client ID Metadata Documents replacing dynamic client registration. Enterprise gateways add API keys, mTLS and per-tool scopes. Reliability Request IDs, error codes, timeouts, cancellation and progress notifications. Make write tools idempotent. Extensibility Capabilities travel in every request's _meta and in server/discover. Optional extensions (tasks, MCP Apps, enterprise-managed auth) add features without changing the core. Design principles Open spec · human-centric (you stay in control) · secure by default · reliable · composable · future-proof. What changed in the 2026-07-28 spec Change What it means Stateless core No initialize handshake and no session ID. Each request carries its protocol version, client info and capabilities in _meta, so servers scale behind ordinary load balancers. State that must persist is passed as explicit handles in tool arguments. server/discover A new method servers must implement, so clients can learn versions and capabilities up front. Multi round-trip requests Instead of calling the client back, a server returns input_required with what it needs (for example an elicitation form); the client retries the request with the answers. Subscriptions subscriptions/listen replaces the HTTP GET stream and resource subscribe/unsubscribe for change notifications. Caching List and read results carry ttlMs and cacheScope, and tools come back in a stable order. Gateway-friendly HTTP Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers on every Streamable HTTP request. Extensions Tasks moved out of the core into an official extension; a formal extensions framework also hosts MCP Apps and enterprise-managed authorization. Deprecated Roots, sampling and logging (use tool parameters, direct model APIs and OpenTelemetry instead), the HTTP+SSE transport, and OAuth dynamic client registration. Deprecated features keep working for at least twelve months. Source: MCP specification changelog, 2026-07-28. See MCP clients for what this means on the wire. Security & governance Authentication Verify clients and servers. Authorization Allow access only to specific capabilities. Encryption Protect data in transit and at rest. Auditing Log every request, response and action. Policy enforcement Rate limits, quotas, allow/deny rules. Common transport & deployment options Option Where it runs Use it for stdio Local subprocess of the host Developer tools, file system, local CLIs. No network exposure. Streamable HTTP Remote service Shared team or SaaS servers, with OAuth and streaming responses. Cloud gateway In front of many servers Central auth, rate limits, routing and audit (see the Gateway Connector role). Message queue Behind a server Long-running or async jobs, where the tool returns a job ID and the result arrives later. ✓ Last reviewed Nov 21, 2026 MCP clients An MCP client is the part of an AI application (the host) that talks to one MCP server. The host runs one client per server connection. Clients don't implement tools: they discover what servers offer, help the model choose, make the requests, handle results and errors, and keep the user in control. This page follows the current specification, 2026-07-28, which made the protocol stateless. The host runs one MCP client per server. Press Play to walk through a request. Reading other MCP infographics? Three common inaccuracies: (1) clients don't search the internet for servers: the host is configured with servers (or picks them from a registry or allowlist), then calls server/discover and the list methods; (2) the standard transports are stdio and Streamable HTTP; WebSocket or message queues are custom or sit behind a server; (3) since 2026-07-28 there is no initialize handshake or session: every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta. How a client works 🔍 1. Discover Optionally call server/discover for versions and capabilities, then list tools, resources and prompts. Cache lists for their ttlMs. 🔗 2. Connect Launch a local server over stdio, or reach a remote one over Streamable HTTP with OAuth. No handshake or session: each request is self-contained. ✅ 3. Select Show the model only the tools policy allows. Filter by server trust, user permissions and task. 📨 4. Request Send tools/call with arguments and _meta (protocol version, client capabilities, client info). Ask the user before risky actions. 📥 5. Receive Handle complete results (validate structured content) and input_required results (ask the user, then retry with the answers). On the wire Pick a message to see what the client sends and gets back (simplified; the spec has every field). Discover List tools Call a tool Input required Retry with input Client sends { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "server/discover", "params": { "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28", "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": { "elicitation": {} }, "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "atlas-agent", "version": "1.4.0" } } } } Server returns { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": { "resultType": "complete", "supportedVersions": ["2026-07-28"], "capabilities": { "tools": {}, "resources": {} }, "serverInfo": { "name": "files-server", "version": "2.1.0" } } } Optional, but useful to pick a protocol version up front. The response shape is simplified here: check the spec for exact fields. Types of MCP clients 💬 Chat apps Assistants that let users connect tools and data, with consent prompts per action. 🤖 Agents Autonomous agents that plan and call tools through MCP, under budgets and policies. 💻 IDEs & dev tools Coding assistants connecting repos, terminals, issue trackers and docs. 🔄 Workflow engines Automation platforms that invoke MCP tools as steps in a pipeline. 📱 Custom apps Any product that wants standard access to external capabilities, built on an MCP SDK. Client readiness checklist Tick what your client does today to see what's missing before production. 0 of 14 in place ⤓ Export checklist Only connects to servers on an allowlist or trusted registry Shows users which server and tool an action uses Asks for approval before write or irreversible tool calls Treats tool descriptions and results as untrusted (injection defenses) Caches list results for their ttlMs instead of polling Validates tool inputs and structured outputs against their schemas Handles input_required results and elicitation UI Echoes requestState untouched and uses a new id on retry Sets timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers Sends protocol version and capabilities in _meta on every request Uses OAuth 2.1 for remote servers and keys credentials by issuer Least-privilege scopes per server Logs and traces every request and response (with redaction) Monitors latency, error rates and usage per server Transports Transport Status Use it for Notes stdio Standard Local servers launched by the host Simple and fast, no network exposure. Log to stderr. Streamable HTTP Standard Remote and shared servers OAuth 2.1; requests carry Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers so gateways can route and rate-limit; stateless, so any instance behind a load balancer can answer. HTTP + SSE Deprecated Older servers only Migrate to Streamable HTTP. WebSocket, queues Custom Special cases Not standard MCP transports. Put async work behind a server (for example the tasks extension), not in the transport. Client vs server MCP client MCP server Role Consumes capabilities on behalf of a host and its model Exposes tools, resources and prompts Starts Every request Nothing on its own; answers requests (and may ask for input via multi round-trip requests) Owns User consent, model context, which servers are trusted The data, the credentials to the real system, the tool logic Offers Elicitation (asking the user); sampling and roots are deprecated Tools, resources, prompts, completions, subscriptions Must guard against Malicious servers: tool-description injection, data exfiltration, over-broad scopes Malicious clients: tampered requestState, abuse, excessive calls Related: Model Context Protocol · MCP protocol deep dive · MCP server roles · AI security. Source: the MCP 2026-07-28 changelog. Key formulas: MCP clients List calls saved by caching calls/hour = 3600 ttl in seconds × servers vs 3600 poll interval × servers Caching list results for their ttlMs instead of polling cuts discovery traffic, and stable tool order keeps the model's prompt cache warm. Servers Poll interval (s) ttlMs (s) = 96 vs 960 list calls per hour Latency with an input-required round trip L = 2· L call + L user A multi round-trip request costs a second call plus however long the user takes to answer. Call latency (ms) User answer time (s) = ≈ 20.8 s Sources & review Time-sensitive · last reviewed Nov 21, 2026 Primary references for the ideas on this page. Figures in calculators come from your own inputs. Model Context Protocol specification IETF RFC 8693, OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange Rechecked: MCP transport and auth spec. Found something out of date? title: Agent dev kit & project structure
text: 🖼 Infographic 7 · Claude Code ✓ Last reviewed Nov 20, 2026 Agent dev kit & project structure CLAUDE.md + Skills + Hooks + Subagents + Plugins. Five layers, each with a different job: CLAUDE.md sets the rules, skills provide expertise, hooks enforce quality, subagents delegate work, and plugins distribute it all to your team. MCP servers and agent teams extend it outward. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. The five layers Layer Role Loaded Lives in Think of it as 1 · CLAUDE.md Memory: architecture rules, naming conventions, test expectations, repo map Always loaded, always active ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (global)./CLAUDE.md ·.claude/CLAUDE.md (project) The agent's constitution 2 · Skills Knowledge: reference docs, scripts, templates On demand, when the description matches the task.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md Modular context chunks. A skill can run in an isolated subagent. 3 · Hooks Guardrails: deterministic checks on events Every matching event settings.json → hooks Git hooks for your agent. Deterministic, not AI. 4 · Subagents Delegation: code-reviewer, test-runner, explorer… When delegated.claude/agents/<name>.md Specialists with their own context window, model, tools and permissions. They can't spawn subagents. 5 · Plugins Distribution: skills/ agents/ hooks/ commands/ Installed once Plugin marketplace / team install npm packages for agent capabilities Hook simulator Event fires → matcher checks → command runs. Pick a scenario to see which hook catches it. Claude runs rm -rf./build / Claude runs npm test Claude writes src/app.ts Session starts Claude finishes its turn code-reviewer subagent finishes Claude reads a file Event fires PreToolUse · Bash Matcher checks matcher "Bash" ✓ Command runs block-dangerous.sh → exit 2 Outcome ⛔ blocked Blocked. The command never runs, and stderr ("refusing recursive delete of /") goes back to Claude so it can adjust. title: Agentic coding & software agents
text: 🖼 Infographic Build & ship · Agentic coding ✓ Last reviewed Nov 23, 2026 Agentic coding & software agents Coding agents read a repository, plan a change, edit files, run the tests and open a pull request. They are the most widely used agents in production, because code gives them something rare: a fast, objective check on their own work. Walk one change from ticket to merge. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. From autocomplete to autonomous Level What it does Human role Typical tasks Completion Suggests the next lines as you type Writes the code Boilerplate, small functions Chat & inline edit Explains or rewrites selected code on request Asks, reviews each change Refactor a function, explain an error Agent in the editor or terminal Runs a multi-step loop in your checkout: search, edit, run, fix Sets the task, watches, approves risky commands Fix a failing test, add an endpoint Background agent Works alone in a cloud sandbox and opens a pull request Reviews the pull request Dependency upgrades, bug backlog, small features Agent fleets Many agents on scheduled or bulk tasks Owns the queue and the review policy Migrations across repositories, flaky-test triage What makes coding agents work Context Instruction files A file at the repository root ( AGENTS.md, or a tool-specific file such as CLAUDE.md) tells every agent how to build, test and lint, the house conventions and what not to touch. AGENTS.md is an open format hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation. Keep it short and keep it true. Specs Spec-driven development For anything bigger than a small fix, write the spec first: goal, constraints, acceptance tests and the files in scope. The agent plans against the spec, a person reviews the plan, then it builds. Specs double as documentation. Feedback Tests are the agent's eyes An agent is only as good as the checks it can run. Fast unit tests, a type checker, a linter and a reproducible build let it find and fix its own mistakes. Repositories with poor tests get confident, wrong changes. Isolation Sandboxes, not laptops Run agents in a container or a throwaway checkout with no production credentials, a network allowlist and a time and token budget. Let them push only to their own branch. Review Review is the new bottleneck Agents write code faster than people can review it. Keep pull requests small, require CI to pass, use an automated reviewer for a first pass, and keep a named person accountable for every merge. Tools Tools, skills & MCP Give agents the tools developers use, through the command line or MCP servers: issue tracker, docs, logs, read-only database access. Package repeated procedures as skills. See Agent dev kit. Good and poor fits Good fit Poor fit (for now) Well-tested code with a clear definition of done Code with no tests or a slow, flaky build Bug fixes with a reproduction Vague product decisions ("make it better") Migrations, upgrades and repetitive refactors New architecture or cross-team design choices Tests, documentation and small features Security-critical code without expert review Exploring and explaining an unfamiliar codebase Changes that can only be checked in production Measuring it Metric What it tells you Watch out for Pull requests merged per agent task Real throughput Counting opened instead of merged Review time and rework The hidden cost on reviewers Large diffs nobody reads closely Change failure rate and rollbacks Quality in production Comparing teams with different work Escaped defects and security findings Risk Agents copying insecure patterns already in the code Cycle time per task type Where time is saved Self-reported savings without a baseline Public benchmarks such as SWE-bench (fixing real GitHub issues) and terminal-task suites help compare models, but they saturate quickly and can leak into training data. Build a small internal set from your own merged pull requests. See Agent evaluation. Risks & controls Prompt injection through code Issues, comments, dependencies and web pages can carry instructions aimed at the agent. Treat repository and web content as untrusted, and never give an agent secrets it doesn't need. Supply chain Agents add dependencies readily, and sometimes invent package names that attackers then register ("slopsquatting"). Pin versions, check new packages against an allowlist and scan every pull request. Destructive commands Block, or require approval for, commands that delete data, force-push, change infrastructure or touch production. Skills atrophy If junior developers never write the code, they never learn to review it. Pair agent use with code reading, design reviews and deliberate practice. Start with one team, one well-tested repository and one task type, for example dependency upgrades. Measure merged pull requests and review time for a month before widening. See ADLC & LLMOps. For long, multi-hour builds, see the three-agent harness (planner, generator, evaluator). Sources & review Time-sensitive · last reviewed Nov 23, 2026 Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: Agent tools & tool calls
text: 🖼 Infographic 2b · Under the hood Agent tools & tool calls The model never runs the tool. It emits a structured tool call (name + arguments), the runtime executes it, and the result goes back into the conversation state as a ToolMessage. The model then reasons over that result and answers. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Conversation state The message list the model sees grows as you step through the flow above. State is empty. Step through the flow to watch messages accumulate. Things that go wrong, and where to catch them Bad arguments The model can hallucinate IDs or send the wrong types. Validate against the JSON Schema before executing, and return a clear error as the ToolMessage so the model can retry. Wrong tool Overlapping tool descriptions cause misrouting. Keep names and descriptions crisp and distinct, and expose only the tools the task needs. Huge results A 5 MB result floods the context. Truncate, paginate or summarize in the tool, not in the model. Side effects Write tools need idempotency keys, approval gates and audit logs. The runtime is the enforcement point, not the prompt. Parallel calls One AIMessage can contain several tool calls. Each result must carry its matching tool_call_id. Loops The model can keep calling tools. Cap the steps and detect repeated identical calls. AI agents need tools A model on its own can only use what it learned in training. Tools let it decide what information is missing and go and get it: search for public facts, query internal data, do exact math, call systems and read web pages. The agent reads the question, picks a tool, inspects the output, repeats if needed, and returns an answer grounded in what the tools returned. Plan → use tools → observe → repeat → answer. Press Play. Walk through one request Step 1 of 6 📥 Read the question "What's the refund policy and can you check if my plan (id 1842) is eligible? Also convert 12.5 hours to minutes." The agent spots three needs: a policy (public), a plan (internal data) and arithmetic. ‹ Back Next › Five essential tools Tool Use it for Example call Watch out for 🔍 Search Public, current information search('latest refund policy') Stale or low-quality sources; cite what you use 🗄 Database Internal structured data SELECT plan FROM users WHERE id = 1842 Read-only credentials; parameterized queries; row-level access 🧮 Calculator / code Exact math and data processing 12.5 * 60 Models do arithmetic unreliably; always compute ☁️ API Actions and data in other systems GET /v1/orders/1842 Auth scopes; write actions need approval and limits 🌐 Browser Pages and apps without an API open(page) → extract table Prompt injection in page content; slow and brittle Related: Tool call anatomy · Tool-using strategies · MCP · Anatomy of an AI agent Tool-using strategies in AI agents Four ways to organize tool calls, each trading cost, latency and control: caching, parallelization, chaining and grouping. Tool caching Parallelization Tool chaining Grouping Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Tool caching Cache the constantly used trajectory (which tool, with what arguments, and the result) to reduce cost and latency. Used in Agentic search, where you constantly call the search API: cache the trajectory. Watch out Stale results. Set TTLs and key the cache on normalized arguments. Latency simulator An agent needs three tool results. Compare running them in sequence, in parallel, or with a warm trajectory cache. Search API 800ms Enterprise DB 500ms Docs API 400ms Cache hit rate 60% Chained (sequential) 1700 ms sum of all calls Parallel 800 ms the slowest call Parallel + cache 332 ms expected: 60% hits at ~20 ms, misses fall back to parallel Chaining is required when a step needs the previous step's output (search location → get flights → update doc). Parallelize only independent calls. Key formulas: Tool-using strategies in AI agents Sequential vs parallel L chain = Σ L i, L parallel = max i L i Parallelize only independent calls. Dependent steps must stay chained. Cache expected latency E[ L ] = h · L hit + (1 − h)· L miss The hit rate h drives the win. A 60% hit rate on an 800 ms call saves about half a second on average. Hit rate Hit ms Miss ms = 332 ms on average (saves 468 ms) Key formulas Expected attempts with validation E[attempts] = 1 p, E[tokens] = T p If a fraction p of tool calls pass schema validation, the expected number of attempts (and tokens) scales with 1/p. Valid on first try Tokens per attempt = 1.18 attempts · ≈ 1,412 tokens Tool-schema overhead T context = T system + Σ tools T schema + T messages Every exposed tool's description is sent on every call. Fifty tools at ~150 tokens each is 7,500 tokens before the user says anything. Tools exposed Tokens per schema = 3,000 tokens of tool definitions per call Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: Workflows & patterns
text: 🖼 Infographic 2c · AI agents Workflows and patterns From rule-based automation to agentic workflows, plus the components of an agent and four core patterns: agentic RAG, tool use, reflection and planning. Pick one to walk through it. Workflow types Components Agentic RAG Tool use Reflection Planning Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Workflow types Automation follows fixed steps. An AI workflow uses a model once. An agentic workflow plans, acts with tools and reflects until the result is OK. Use it for Use the least autonomy that solves the problem. Fixed steps are cheapest and most predictable. LLM workflow patterns Design smarter pipelines, get better results. Five composable patterns: chain, parallelization, routing, orchestrator–workers and evaluator–optimizer. In these, your code (or the orchestrator) controls the flow. Reach for a fully autonomous agent only when none of them fit. 1 Chain 2 Parallelization 3 Routing 4 Orchestrator–workers 5 Evaluator–optimizer Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. 1 · Chain workflow Break a complex task into a sequence of simple, dependent steps. A programmatic gate between steps can stop bad output early. When to use Tasks with clear sequential steps Trading latency for higher accuracy Each step builds on the previous output Which pattern fits? Steps are fixed and happen in order Different input types need different handling Independent pieces can run at the same time Subtasks can only be decided after seeing the input There are clear criteria, and revision improves results → Chain Show Chain ↑ These are the workflow patterns described in Anthropic's Building effective agents guide. They compose: a router can send a request into a chain, and a chain's step can be an evaluator–optimizer loop. Key formulas: LLM workflow patterns Majority voting (parallelization) P (correct) = Σ k > n /2 C( n, k) p k (1− p) n − k n independent voters, each right with probability p. If p is above 0.5, more voters help (assuming their errors are independent). Voter accuracy p Voters n (odd) = 89.6% vs 75% for a single call Routing savings C routed = c router + Σ j s j · c j Send the share s of easy traffic to a cheap model and pay the big model only where needed. Easy share Big model $ / call Small model $ / call Router $ / call = $0.0097 vs $0.0200 → 51.5% cheaper Key formulas Reflection: diminishing returns q t+1 = q t + α·(1 − q t) Each critique closes a fraction α of the remaining gap, so gains shrink every round. Two or three rounds usually capture most of the value. Initial quality α (gain per round) Rounds = after 3 rounds: 89% Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: Reference architecture & the AI OS
text: 🖼 Infographic 5b · Reference Reference architecture & the AI OS Nine layers of a production agentic system: goal-driven, multi-agent, orchestrated, observable and reliable. Step through a request end to end, or click any layer for details. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Layer by layer 1 · User / client layer Web and mobile apps, chat and voice, API/SDK, enterprise systems. Requests enter here, and responses (often streamed) return here. 2 · Orchestration / control plane The orchestrator or workflow engine: planner, router, scheduler, policy enforcer. It handles task decomposition, agent selection, plan and execution management, state and context management, and guardrails and policy. 3 · Agent layer Specialized agents: research (search, analyze), reasoning (reason, plan), action (execute, call tools), data (query, process) and communication (summarize, communicate). 4 · Tools & integrations Web search, APIs, code execution, databases, file and document processing, other services. Usually exposed through MCP. 5 · Memory & knowledge Short-term memory (context), long-term memory (vector DB), knowledge base (docs), episodic/event store (history), user and org profile store. 6 · Monitoring & observability End-to-end tracing and logging, metrics and dashboards (latency, tokens, cost), alerts on anomalies and failures, audit and compliance logs. 7 · Reliability & failure management Error detection, retry with backoff, fallback or alternate agents, human-in-the-loop, circuit breakers. 8 · Governance & security Authentication and authorization, data privacy and PII protection, policy enforcement, model and prompt guardrails, compliance and audit. 9 · Foundation / infrastructure LLM providers, model gateway (routing, rate limits, cost management), vector DB, data storage, queue/event bus, cache, secrets manager, CI/CD and deployment. The AI operating system A prompt that goes in and a response that comes out breaks on complex tasks. Reliable agents need a runtime around the model, the way programs need an operating system: memory, a planner, a scheduler, a tool router, an evaluator and an interface, connected by a knowledge graph of entities and relationships. The loop becomes plan → act → evaluate → improve. The future isn't only bigger models; it's better systems. Six components around a knowledge graph. Press Play. What breaks without each component Switch a component off to see the failure it would cause. ✓ Memory ✓ Planner ✓ Scheduler ✓ Tool router ✓ Evaluator ✓ Interface ✓ Knowledge graph All components running: plan → act → evaluate → improve. Click one to switch it off. Traditional AI vs an AI operating system Prompt → response AI operating system Flow One pass Plan → act → evaluate → improve, repeated State Only what's in the prompt Memory and a knowledge graph persist across steps and sessions Failures Returned to the user Detected by the evaluator; retried or rerouted by the scheduler Actions None, or ad hoc Through a tool router with permissions and limits Fits Single questions Multi-step, long-running, reliable autonomous work Related: AXIS, an agentic OS (my frameworks) · Anatomy of an AI agent · Agents in production · Harness engineering · AI system design: six layers Key formulas Availability: series vs redundant A series = Π A i, A redundant = 1 − Π (1 − A i) Layers in series multiply availability down. A fallback model or route in parallel multiplies the failure rate down instead. Component availability Layers in series = series 94.1% · with one redundant pair 100% Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page.
