title: Automation vs digital workers vs agents
text: 🖼 Infographic Agents · Choosing the approach Automation, digital workers & AI agents Three ways to get work done by software, from most predictable to most flexible. Automation follows fixed rules and triggers. A digital worker follows a defined workflow (understand → process → execute → record) with AI inside some steps, validations at each one and a full log. An AI agent decides its own path. Most real systems combine all three: automation for the routine, digital workers for structured judgment, agents for the exceptions. A typical invoice process: automation for the routine, a digital worker for structured judgment, an agent for exceptions. Press Play. Side by side ⚙️ Automation 🧾 Digital worker 🤖 AI agent How it works Rules and triggers A defined workflow with AI steps and checks Perceives, reasons and chooses its own steps Path Same every time Same steps, AI handles variation inside them May differ every time Handles Structured, repetitive work Semi-structured work: documents, emails, forms Open-ended, novel or multi-step problems Traceability Full Full: every step logged and auditable Needs tracing; reasoning is harder to audit Consistency Very high High Variable without evals and guardrails Improves by Someone changing the rules Tuning steps, prompts and validations Better prompts, tools, memory and evals (it doesn't learn on its own unless you build that in) Cost to start Low Medium Higher, plus per-run model cost Which fits your task? 1. Are the steps the same every time? Always Mostly, with variation inside steps No, it varies per case 2. What are the inputs like? Structured fields Documents, emails, forms Anything; often novel 3. How much judgment is needed? None: rules decide Some: classify, extract, match A lot: investigate, plan, decide 4. How important is a full audit trail? Critical Important Nice to have 5. Volume? Very high Medium Low, high-value cases 6. Cost of a wrong action? Severe Moderate Low and reversible Related: Where agents fit · Automation pipelines · Agentic process automation vs RPA · Architecture decision wizard Where do AI agents actually fit? A practical map for deciding when to deploy an agent, and when to leave the task alone. Fits: bounded, reviewable, goal-directed tasks. Doesn't fit: irreversible, ambiguous, high-stakes calls. Press Play or Next to walk through the flow. Click any box for details. Fit checker Answer five questions about a task you have in mind. Do the steps vary from case to case? Yes No Can success be checked with a clear pass/fail signal? Yes No Is every action reversible, or reviewed before it takes effect? Yes No Can you log and audit what it did? Yes No Is this a high-stakes judgment call with no precedent? Yes No Good agent fit. Start narrow (month 1), then widen once the error rate is measured. Agents vs automation Automation follows a fixed script: same steps every time, no judgment calls. An agent is given a goal, plans its own steps, uses tools and adapts. Rule of thumb: if the steps never change, automate it; if the path varies, an agent may help. Where agents actually help Research and synthesis Triage and routing Drafting that gets revised Monitoring and flagging Where agents still fail Irreversible actions: payments, deletions, signed contracts Tasks with no clear definition of success Judgment calls with no precedent Anything you can't audit afterwards A rollout timeline Month 1 · one bounded task with a clear pass/fail signal → Month 2 · give it tool access, human reviews every output → Months 3–6 · widen scope once the error rate is measured and low; review becomes spot-check, then exception-only The honest trade-off An agent trades your direct control of each step for speed across many steps. That only pays off inside a defined boundary. Narrow scope: one task, clear rules, quick to trust. Wide scope: many tasks, vague rules, hard to trust or debug. Value follows intent, not the number of agents you deploy. Avoid these mistakes Production access before testing No handoff back to a human Vague or unmeasured success No logs to review after the fact Key formulas: Where do AI agents actually fit? Is the agent worth it? V = N · t saved · w − N · e · c error − C run − C build Monthly value: time saved minus the cost of errors, run cost and amortized build cost. If e·c_error is large (irreversible tasks), keep a human at the exit. Tasks / month Hours saved / task $ / hour Error rate $ per error Run $ / month Build $ / month = +$15,700 per month ✓ worth it Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: AI project-building workflow
text: 🖼 Infographic Learn · Build with AI The AI project-building workflow Idea → plan → build → test → showcase. For students and early-career builders: use AI to go faster without handing over the understanding. The goal isn't a repo for GitHub; it's a project you can understand, explain and defend in an interview. Your project: 0 of 32 checkpoints done ⤓ Export my plan 1. Define the problem 2. Plan the MVP 3. Research the stack 4. Design before coding 5. Build in small features 6. Debug + test 7. Document 8. Showcase + improve 1. Define the problem What problem am I solving? Who has it? Why does it matter? What is the smallest useful version? Problem in one sentence Target user named Why it matters written down Smallest useful version defined Prompt to try: Help me clarify this project idea. Identify the target user, problem, assumptions and a possible MVP. Don't design the entire project for me. Project idea filter Does it solve a real problem? Can I build a small MVP? Will I learn something? Can I explain the technology? Can I demonstrate the result? Can I improve it later? Pick a different idea, or shrink it. 0 of 6 yes AI can help / you own AI can help with Brainstorming Architecture feedback Documentation Debugging Code explanations Test-case generation Refactoring suggestions You own Product decisions Core understanding Verification Technical choices Testing Explaining it AI assists the build. You own the project. MVP formula One user · one problem · one core feature · one working flow. Don't build 20 features nobody needs. 4-week plan Week 1: problem, research, MVP Week 2: architecture and core feature Week 3: testing and improvements Week 4: docs, deployment, showcase Interview test Why did you build it? Why this tech stack? How does it work? What was the hardest bug? What would you improve? Don't Build a huge project immediately Copy AI code you don't understand Use tools you can't explain Skip testing Commit secrets or API keys Put a project on your résumé you can't explain Debugging loop Reproduce → read the error → isolate → form a hypothesis → test → fix → test again → document. Don't paste errors into AI blindly: understand what failed. Responsible AI use Understand generated code Verify dependencies and docs Never expose API keys Check licenses Follow academic rules; say when AI helped Related: Study smarter with AI · AI career paths · AI & LLM roadmaps Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: About this Atlas
text: 🖼 Infographic Start here · About About the AI Architecture Atlas A free, interactive guide to how modern AI systems are designed, built, governed and paid for. It is written for four kinds of reader at once: executives deciding where AI fits, customers and business owners scoping a project, forward-deployed engineers delivering one, and anyone learning the field from scratch. Who builds it Created and maintained by Rakesh, Director of AI for Forward-Deployed Engineering, leading a team that delivers generative, agentic and voice AI for enterprises. Before that, he built and ran an automation practice across the US and India. He holds a Master's in Electrical Engineering and created the ABL and AGIL frameworks described in this Atlas. Views are his own and don't represent any employer or vendor. Why it exists Most AI material is either a vendor pitch or a research paper. Teams need something in between: the patterns that actually ship, drawn as systems you can step through, with the numbers, risks and decisions that sit around them. Every page tries to answer three questions: how does it work, when should I use it, and what goes wrong. How it stays honest Sources are listed at the bottom of every page. Prefer the primary source: specs, standards, papers and official docs. Time-sensitive pages (protocols, regulations, products) carry a "last reviewed" badge and are rechecked monthly; see What's changed. No invented statistics. Figures come from a named source or from a calculator where you enter your own numbers. Where a popular infographic gets something wrong, the page says so. Vendor neutrality The patterns are vendor-neutral: RAG, agents, MCP, A2A, evaluation and governance work the same on any model or platform. Product names appear as examples, not endorsements. The hands-on pages use Claude because the Atlas itself runs on it, so every "try it" button works in place; the same steps apply to other assistants. title: Contact-center AI architecture
text: 🖼 Infographic Customer service AI · Architecture ✓ Last reviewed Nov 21, 2026 Contact-center AI reference architecture Customer service is where most enterprises meet AI at scale. A modern contact center puts an AI layer across every channel: a virtual agent resolves what it safely can, hands off to a person with full context when it can't, assists the human during the conversation, and analyzes 100% of conversations afterwards. Step through one customer journey below. A customer contacts support. Follow the conversation through routing, the virtual agent, handoff, assist and analytics. Press Play. The layers 📞 Channels Voice (phone, IVR), web and in-app chat, messaging (SMS, WhatsApp), email and social. Each has different latency, length and compliance rules, but they should share one conversation record. 🔀 Routing & identity Identify and verify the customer, detect intent and urgency, and decide: virtual agent, a specific queue, or a priority human. Routing uses the customer's history, not just the words of the first message. 🤖 Virtual agent An LLM with retrieval over policies and knowledge, tools for the customer's own data (orders, bookings, balances), and deterministic flows where steps must happen exactly (authentication, payments, disclosures). 🤝 Handoff Escalation with a context packet: who the customer is, what they asked, what was tried, sentiment, and the suggested next step. The customer never repeats themselves. See assist & handoff. 🧑‍💼 Agent assist Real-time help for the human: suggested answers with sources, next-best action, form filling, compliance reminders and an automatic after-call summary. 📊 Analytics & QA Every conversation transcribed, summarized, tagged and scored against a QA rubric; trends feed back into knowledge, flows and coaching. See QA & omnichannel. Design rules that matter Rule Why Deterministic where it must be, generative where it helps Identity verification, payments, legally required disclosures and cancellations follow fixed flows. Explaining a policy, troubleshooting and summarizing are where LLMs shine. Always offer a way out A clear route to a human at any point. Trapping customers in a bot loop destroys satisfaction faster than anything else. Ground every answer Answers come from approved knowledge and the customer's own records, never the model's memory. No source → say so and hand off. Voice is its own discipline Latency budgets under about a second per turn, barge-in, short answers, spelling of names and numbers, and DTMF fallback. See voice agent layers. Measure resolution, not deflection A contained conversation where the customer calls back tomorrow is a failure. See metrics. Compliance by channel Call recording consent, AI disclosure rules, outbound calling rules (such as the US TCPA), PCI DSS for card data and data retention limits differ by channel and country. title: CX metrics & value calculator
text: 🖼 Infographic Customer service AI · Business case Contact-center AI metrics & value calculator The contact-center business case rests on a handful of metrics: containment (resolved without a person), average handle time (AHT) for what still reaches a person, first-contact resolution (FCR) and customer satisfaction (CSAT). Enter your own numbers; nothing here uses industry benchmarks you can't verify. Contacts per month Share entering self-service (%) Resolved containment (%) Cost per live contact ($) Cost per automated contact ($) AHT today (minutes) AHT reduction from assist (%) Paid hours per agent per month Occupancy (%) Shrinkage (%) 21,000 contacts resolved by AI / month 79,000 contacts still reaching people $1,360,800 yearly cost difference on resolved contacts 37.6 agent FTE of workload removed Workload drops from 11,667 to 8,295 handled hours a month. This is a gross figure: subtract platform, implementation, knowledge upkeep and QA costs (use the ROI tools), and expect containment to ramp up over months. If repeat contacts rise, your resolved containment is lower than you entered. Definitions that hold up in a review Metric Formula Watch out for Containment rate contacts ended in self-service ÷ contacts that entered self-service Counts abandonment as success. Report resolved containment instead. Resolved containment contained contacts with no repeat contact on the same issue within N days ÷ entered Pick N (often 3–7 days) and keep it fixed. Average handle time (talk + hold + after-call work) ÷ handled contacts Automation removes easy contacts, so AHT on what remains can rise even as total workload falls. First-contact resolution issues resolved with no repeat contact within N days ÷ issues Needs an issue key to link repeat contacts across channels. CSAT satisfied responses (4–5 of 5) ÷ responses Survey bias: unhappy and bot-abandoning customers often skip surveys. Transfer rate virtual-agent conversations handed to a person ÷ virtual-agent conversations Low isn't always good; it can mean customers are stuck. Cost per contact total channel cost ÷ contacts Include platform, LLM usage, telephony, people, QA and knowledge upkeep. Occupancy & FTE FTE ≈ workload hours ÷ (paid hours × occupancy × (1 − shrinkage)) Savings arrive through attrition and hiring avoided, not overnight. Key formulas Resolved containment C res = N contained − N repeat N entered Contacts that stayed in self-service and did not come back on the same issue within N days, over all contacts that entered self-service. Entered self-service Contained Repeat contacts within N days = 35% resolved containment (vs 45% raw) Average handle time AHT = T + H + W N handled Talk, hold and after-call work time divided by contacts handled by people. Talk minutes (total) Hold minutes After-call work minutes Handled contacts = 7 minutes per contact First-contact resolution FCR = N issues − N repeat issues N issues Issues resolved without a repeat contact within the window, across all channels. Issues Issues with a repeat contact = 76% FCR Agent FTE from workload FTE = N · AHT / 60 P · o · (1 − s) Workload hours divided by productive hours per agent: paid hours × occupancy × (1 − shrinkage). Contacts handled / month AHT minutes Paid hours / agent / month Occupancy Shrinkage = 78.1 FTE Self-service cost difference ΔC = N resolved · ( c live − c auto) · 12 Yearly gross difference from contacts resolved by AI instead of people; subtract platform and run costs for the net figure. Resolved by AI / month $ per live contact $ per automated contact = $1,360,800 per year (gross) Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: Agent assist & handoff
text: 🖼 Infographic Customer service AI · Human + AI Agent assist & live-agent handoff The best customer-service AI makes the human better, not absent. Two moments decide the experience: the handoff, where the virtual agent passes the customer to a person without making them repeat themselves, and assist, where AI helps that person in real time and writes up the conversation afterwards. What happens in the seconds around a handoff. Press Play. When should the virtual agent hand off? Tick what's true about the conversation so far. The rules reflect common policy; set your own thresholds in production. Customer asked for a person Always honor it, immediately. High-risk topic (complaint, legal, vulnerability, bereavement, fraud) Policy: route to a trained person. Virtual agent failed twice on the same step Repeated failure is the strongest predictor of a bad experience. Sentiment is negative and getting worse Combine with other signals. Low confidence in understanding the request Ask one clarifying question first. Needs an action the virtual agent isn't permitted to do Hand off with the action pre-filled. High-value or at-risk customer Prioritize in the queue rather than forcing handoff. Conversation over 10 turns Long loops usually mean the bot is stuck. Continue · handoff score 0/100 Keep going with the virtual agent; the customer can still ask for a person at any time. The context packet What travels with the customer Verified identity and authentication level Intent, the customer's own words, and the summary so far What the virtual agent tried and the result Records looked up (order, account, case number) Sentiment trend and the reason for handoff Suggested next step for the human Agent assist during the conversation Knowledge surfacing: answers with the source article, not just text Next-best action: the step policy suggests now Compliance prompts: required disclosures, prohibited phrases Form and CRM filling from the conversation After-call work: summary, disposition, follow-up tasks Measure assist by what changes for agents: after-call work time, time to proficiency for new hires, and how often suggestions are accepted. Low acceptance usually means poor knowledge, not lazy agents. Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: IVR & legacy bot migration
h1: From IVR & legacy bots to LLM agents
text: 🖼 Infographic Customer service AI · Modernization From IVR & legacy bots to LLM agents Most organizations already have an IVR menu and an intent-based chatbot. Replacing them in one go is risky; migrating intent by intent, with the old system as a safety net, is not. The plan below moves from logs to shadow mode to live traffic, and the scorer helps you decide what each intent should become. Move from IVR and intent bots to an LLM agent without a big-bang cutover. Press Play. Intent treatment scorer Rate an intent on four factors. The result suggests whether it should stay a fixed flow, become an LLM-handled intent with guardrails, or go straight to a person. Intent Volume 3/5 Rare Top-10 intent How varied are the requests? 3/5 Always the same steps Every case differs Data the bot needs 2/5 None or public Many systems Risk if wrong 2/5 Low Money, legal or safety Order status: LLM agent with guardrails Varied requests where explanation helps: ground it in approved knowledge, give it scoped tools and keep fixed flows for authentication and payments. Medium priority. Migration plan Phase What happens Exit criterion 1 · Assess Mine call and chat logs: top intents by volume, current containment and transfer per intent, failure reasons, dead-end menu paths. Ranked intent list with baselines 2 · Shadow The LLM agent sees live conversations but doesn't answer; its responses are scored against what happened. Agreed quality bar met on a golden set 3 · Hybrid LLM handles open questions and understanding; fixed flows still run authentication and transactions. Start with a share of traffic. Resolved containment and CSAT at or above baseline 4 · Expand Add intents and channels one at a time; voice usually after chat. Each intent passes its own gate 5 · Retire Decommission menus and intents the new system has replaced; keep a fallback path for outages. No traffic on retired paths for an agreed period Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: QA at scale & omnichannel
text: 🖼 Infographic Customer service AI · Quality QA at scale & omnichannel continuity Traditional QA reviews a tiny sample of conversations by hand. With transcription and an LLM judge you can score every conversation against the same rubric, then spend human time calibrating the judge and coaching. The same conversation record is what lets a customer move from chat to phone without starting over. From recording to coaching. Press Play. Build a QA rubric Pick the criteria that matter for your operation, set weights and mark the ones that fail a conversation automatically. Export it as the judge prompt. Criterion Weight Auto-fail Greeting & identification Correct greeting; identity verified before account details Understood the issue Restated or confirmed the customer's goal Accurate answer Information matches policy and the customer's records Resolution Issue resolved, or a clear next step and timeline Compliance Required disclosures made; no prohibited statements Empathy & tone Acknowledged feelings; professional, plain language Efficiency No unnecessary holds, transfers or repetition Data handling Didn't read out or request unnecessary personal data Total weight 110 (aim for 100) ⤓ Judge prompt Omnichannel continuity One customer Identity resolution links phone number, email, app login and chat cookie to one profile, with consent and verification rules per channel. One conversation A shared conversation record (summary, open case, last step) follows the customer. A switch from chat to voice opens with "I see you were asking about…". Channel-fit answers The same answer is shaped per channel: short and spoken for voice, links and buttons for chat, full detail for email. Calibrate the judge before trusting it: double-score a sample each week with experienced QA analysts and track agreement. See LLM as a judge. title: Discovery kit
text: 🖼 Infographic FDE kit · Week one Discovery kit The first week decides the project. Use this kit to run discovery the same way every time: the questions to ask, who to ask, and the documents to collect. Tick what you've covered, add notes, and export a requirements brief to share with the customer. Customer Use case 0/30 questions covered · 0/8 documents collected Question bank Business & outcomes 0/5 What problem are we solving, and for whom? How is it measured today, and what is the baseline? What does success look like in 90 days? In a year? Who is the executive sponsor, and what do they need to see? What is the cost of doing nothing? Users & process 0/5 Who are the users, how many, and in which channels and languages? Walk me through the process today, step by step. Where does it break? Which steps need human judgment or approval? What are the top requests by volume? What happens when things go wrong today? Data & knowledge 0/5 Where does the knowledge live, who owns it, and how current is it? Which systems hold the records the AI must read or update? Is there personal, payment or health data involved? Who can see what? How are permissions managed? Do we have real examples (transcripts, tickets) to build a test set? Systems & integration 0/5 Which systems need integration, and do they have APIs? What identity provider is used for sign-in? Are there existing bots, IVRs or automations to replace or coexist with? What environments exist (dev, test, prod), and how do releases work? Any network, residency or vendor restrictions? Risk, security & compliance 0/5 Which regulations apply (industry, privacy, AI-specific)? What must the AI never do or say? Which actions are irreversible and need confirmation? Who signs off on security and privacy reviews, and how long do they take? What is the incident and escalation process? Delivery & ownership 0/5 Who owns the solution after go-live? Who maintains knowledge and answers? What is the budget and timeline, and what is fixed? What are the dependencies on other teams? How will we decide to go live (quality gate)? Stakeholder map Who to meet in week one, and what each one cares about. title: Enterprise integration patterns
text: 🖼 Infographic FDE kit · Integration Enterprise integration patterns An agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach. Most enterprise work happens in CRM, ITSM, ERP and HR systems; reaching them safely means picking the right pattern, and making sure the agent acts as the user, with that user's permissions, rather than as an all-powerful service account. The user signs in once; every tool call carries that user's permissions. Press Play. Pick the pattern Pattern How it works Use when Watch out for Tool over API The agent calls a typed tool, often exposed through an MCP server, that wraps the system's REST or GraphQL API. The system has a documented API. The default choice. Rate limits, pagination, and tools that are too broad Event-driven The system emits webhooks or events (case created, order shipped); the agent reacts or updates the conversation. Proactive notifications, long-running processes Ordering, retries and duplicate events (make handlers idempotent) iPaaS / integration hub The agent calls one integration layer that already connects many systems. The customer already runs an integration platform An extra hop in latency; who owns the flows Data sync for retrieval Content is synced into a search index with permissions attached. Read-heavy questions over documents and records Freshness and permission drift between source and index UI automation (RPA) A bot drives the system's screens. Legacy systems with no API, as a last resort Brittle when screens change; slow; hard to secure Common systems System type Examples Typical agent actions CRM Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics, HubSpot Look up a customer or case, log an interaction, update an opportunity ITSM / service desk ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, Zendesk Create or update a ticket, check status, search the knowledge base ERP / commerce SAP, Oracle, Shopify Order status, returns, invoices, inventory HR Workday, SuccessFactors Leave balance, policy questions, onboarding tasks Contact center Genesys, NICE, Amazon Connect, Five9 Transfer with context, read queue state, write dispositions Identity: act as the user Do Sign users in with the customer's identity provider (SSO with OIDC or SAML) Call systems with a token for that user: OAuth on-behalf-of or token exchange (RFC 8693) Scope each tool to the least privilege it needs Log every call with the user, the agent and the tool Avoid One admin service account for all users: the agent can then read what the user can't Long-lived API keys inside prompts or tool code Letting the model choose which identity to use Writes without a confirmation step for anything irreversible Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: Privacy engineering
text: 🖼 Infographic FDE kit · Data protection Privacy engineering for AI Personal data flows through prompts, logs, indexes and evaluation sets. Privacy engineering decides where it is removed, where it is replaced with tokens that can be reversed only by authorized code, where it is stored and for how long, and who can retrieve it. Where personal data is detected, replaced, used and kept. Press Play. Try redaction A simple pattern-based redactor running in your browser. Production systems combine patterns with trained entity recognizers (for example, Microsoft Presidio) and test both on real samples. Hi, this is Maria Lopez. My account #48213977 was charged twice. Card 4111 1111 1111 1111, exp 09/28. Call me at (407) 555-0142 or maria.lopez@example.com. DOB 03/14/1986. Tokenize Mask Remove Hi, this is Maria Lopez. My <ACCOUNT_1> was charged twice. Card <CARD_1>, exp 09/28. Call me at <PHONE_1> or <EMAIL_1> DOB <DATE_1>. Token (what the model sees) Original (kept in the vault) <EMAIL_1> maria.lopez@example.com. <CARD_1> 4111 1111 1111 1111 <PHONE_1> (407) 555-0142 <ACCOUNT_1> account #48213977 <DATE_1> 03/14/1986 Note what it misses: the name "Maria Lopez" isn't caught by patterns. That's why production redaction adds entity recognition, and why you test on real samples. Decisions to make with the customer Decision Options Notes Redact or tokenize Remove · mask · reversible token Tokenize when the agent must act on the value later (e.g. look up an account) without the model seeing it. Data residency Region-pinned model endpoints, storage and logs Check where prompts, outputs, embeddings and traces are processed, not just stored. Retention Transcripts, logs, traces, eval sets Set a period per data type; make deletion requests reach indexes and backups. Provider data use Training opt-out, zero data retention options Get it in the contract, not just a settings page. Permission-aware retrieval Filter by user's access before ranking Carry access lists on every chunk and filter before the model sees anything. Legal basis GDPR, HIPAA, GLBA, PCI DSS, local laws Involve the customer's privacy officer early; record the basis per purpose. title: Observability & on-call
text: 🖼 Infographic FDE kit · Run it ✓ Last reviewed Nov 21, 2026 Observability & on-call for AI agents You can't fix what you can't see. Trace every request end to end, from the user message through retrieval, model calls and tools, using a shared vocabulary so any backend can read it. OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions provide that vocabulary; they moved to their own repository in June 2026 and are still marked Development, so pin a version. One request, as a trace Click a span to see the attributes you'd record. invoke_agent support-agent 2900 ms retrieval kb-search 320 ms chat (plan) 700 ms execute_tool get_order 450 ms chat (answer) 1100 ms guardrail output-check 70 ms Attribute Example gen_ai.operation.name invoke_agent gen_ai.agent.name support-agent gen_ai.conversation.id conv_8f2a Attribute names follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions (status: Development). Plain names such as operation are illustrative. Don't record prompt or response content by default: it's opt-in and may contain personal data. Dashboards & alerts Signal Source Alert when Latency (p50/p95, time to first token) gen_ai.client.operation.duration p95 above the experience budget for 10 minutes Tokens & cost gen_ai.client.token.usage by model and feature Daily spend above forecast; sudden jump per conversation Errors Span status, error.type Error rate above baseline; provider rate limits Tool failures Tool spans ( execute_tool) A tool failing for more than N% of calls Quality Online eval scores, thumbs-down, escalations Groundedness or CSAT drop versus last week Safety Guardrail blocks, PII detections Any spike; any confirmed leak (page immediately) On-call runbook 1 · Triage Is it the provider, a tool, retrieval or a change we shipped? Check the provider status page, recent deploys and prompt or model changes. 2 · Contain Fail over to a backup model, disable the failing tool, switch to a safe fixed flow, or route to people. Have these switches ready before launch. 3 · Learn Add the failing conversations to the regression set, fix, and write a short post-incident note. See the incident register. title: Conversation regression testing
text: 🖼 Infographic FDE kit · Quality Regression testing for conversations A conversational agent changes whenever its prompt, model, knowledge or tools change. Regression testing catches what broke: a golden set of real conversations with expected outcomes, simulated users that probe edge cases, and coverage across languages and channels. Run it on every change, and block release when it fails. Plan your test suite Intents in scope Golden conversations per intent Simulated personas Languages Channels (chat, voice…) Runs per sim (to catch randomness) 240 golden conversations to curate 576 simulated conversations per full run 72 smoke set for every commit (3 per intent) ⤓ Test suite skeleton (YAML) What to assert Outcome Did the conversation reach the right end state: resolved, correct handoff, correct tool call with correct arguments? Content Is the answer grounded in the right source, complete and free of prohibited statements? Use code checks first, an LLM judge second. Experience Turns to resolution, tone, length per channel, latency per turn, and whether the customer had to repeat themselves. Simulated users are another LLM playing a customer persona with a goal and a hidden fact. Vary patience, clarity, language and mood. Review a sample by hand: simulated customers are often more cooperative than real ones. Key formulas Simulated conversations per run S = I · P · L · C · R Intents × personas × languages × channels × repeated runs (to catch randomness). Intents Personas Languages Channels Runs per case = 576 simulated conversations Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: Handover & enablement
text: 🖼 Infographic FDE kit · Go-live & after Handover & customer enablement A project isn't done when it goes live; it's done when the customer can run it without you. Plan hypercare, train the people who will own it, agree who does what, and leave a runbook they can actually use. title: Data readiness assessment
text: 🖼 Infographic Architecture · Before you build Data readiness assessment Most AI projects that slip, slip on data, not models. Before choosing an architecture, check every data source the use case needs on six questions: can we reach it, is it accurate, is it complete and current, who owns it and who may see it, may we legally use it this way, and do we have real examples to test against. Score each source below; the result tells you what is ready, what can be fixed in weeks, and what blocks the project. Use case + Add data source 2 sources · 0 ready · 0 blocking Data source Access Quality Coverage & freshness Ownership & permissions Legal basis Test examples Result Fixable in weeks ✕ Fixable in weeks ✕ Ready with a data workstream Nothing blocks, but plan the fixes below as a workstream in the first weeks, with owners and dates. Actions, most urgent first CRM customer records · Test examples (0/3): Collect 50–200 real, redacted examples with the outcome you expect; label them with the business owner. Knowledge base articles · Coverage & freshness (1/3): Fill coverage gaps with the business owner; set a sync schedule and an owner for updates. Knowledge base articles · Test examples (1/3): Collect 50–200 real, redacted examples with the outcome you expect; label them with the business owner. CRM customer records · Legal basis (1/3): Take it to privacy and legal now: confirm the lawful basis, consent and contract terms for this purpose. ⤓ Readiness report (Markdown) What each kind of AI needs from your data Approach Data it needs Most common gap Prompt + model Good examples of inputs and desired outputs No agreed "good answer" to test against RAG / knowledge assistant Documents with structure, owners, dates and access lists Outdated or duplicate documents; no permissions metadata Agents with tools APIs to the systems of record, test accounts, clear business rules No API, or only an all-powerful service account Customer service AI Transcripts and tickets with outcomes, intent labels, knowledge base Recordings without consent for reuse; no outcome labels Prediction & forecasting Clean history with the outcome you want to predict Too little history, or the process changed recently Fine-tuning Hundreds to thousands of high-quality labeled examples Examples that encode today's mistakes Key formulas Source readiness R = min( s access, …, s eval); blocker if s access = 0 or s legal = 0 A source is only as ready as its weakest dimension (0–3); no access path or no legal basis blocks it outright. Access (0–3) Quality Freshness Ownership Legal basis Test examples = Fixable: weakest dimension 1/3 Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. title: AI operating model & workforce
text: 🖼 Infographic CAIO · Organization & people AI operating model, roles & workforce Strategy says what to do with AI; the operating model says who does it and how decisions get made. Three choices matter most: how centralized the AI team is, which roles you hire or grow, and how you bring the rest of the workforce along. Most AI programs that stall have the technology working and the organization not. Pick an operating model Centralized CoE One AI team builds and runs everything for the business. + Consistent standards, scarce talent pooled, fast start − Becomes a bottleneck; far from the business Fits: early maturity, small or highly regulated organizations Hub-and-spoke A central hub owns platform, governance and standards; teams in the business units build on it. + Scale with guardrails; business ownership − Needs clear decision rights and funding rules Fits: most mid-to-large organizations once past the first pilots Federated Each business unit runs its own AI teams; a small central group sets policy. + Speed and closeness to the business − Duplicated platforms, uneven quality and risk Fits: high maturity, very autonomous business units Which fits you now? Organization size AI maturity Business-unit autonomy Regulatory pressure Suggested: Hub-and-spoke Keep platform, governance and evaluation central; fund and staff builders inside the business units, with clear decision rights. Operating models evolve: most organizations move from central to hub-and-spoke as maturity grows. Roles to hire or grow Role Owns When you need it AI leader / CAIO Strategy, portfolio, value, risk appetite, executive alignment From the start AI product manager Use case outcomes, users, success metrics, roadmap per product First production use case AI / ML engineer Prompts, retrieval, agents, model integration, evaluation code First build Forward-deployed engineer / solution architect Turning a business process into a working system with the users When use cases span many teams or customers Data engineer Pipelines, quality, access, lineage for AI data As soon as data readiness has gaps Evaluation & QA lead Test sets, judges, release gates, production quality Before the first go-live AI risk & governance lead Policy, inventory, impact assessments, regulatory mapping Before the first customer-facing or high-risk use Knowledge curator Content the AI answers from: accuracy, freshness, ownership Any knowledge assistant or customer service AI Change & enablement lead Training, communications, adoption measurement Before rollout to more than one team Redesign work, task by task AI changes tasks, not whole jobs. List the tasks in one role, estimate the hours and pick the kind of work; the tool suggests what to automate, what to augment and what to keep human. Role + Task Task Hours / week Kind of work Suggested Augment (AI drafts, person checks) ✕ Augment (AI drafts, person edits) ✕ Keep human (AI informs) ✕ Augment (AI drafts, person edits) ✕ Keep human ✕ Automate ✕ 31 hours per week in these tasks ≈ 7.9 hours a week AI could free (rough planning factors) 25% of this time Planning factors, not measurements: routine 70%, information 40%, drafting 30%, judgment 10%, relationships 0%. Replace them with what your pilot measures. Bring the workforce along AI literacy, in four tiers Everyone: what AI is and isn't, approved tools, data rules, how to check output Power users: prompting, building personal workflows, spotting failure modes Builders: RAG, agents, evaluation, security by design Leaders: value cases, risk appetite, redesigning work, leading change Adoption playbook Explain why, and what it means for each role, before the tools arrive Start with willing teams and visible quick wins Name champions in every team; give them time, not just titles Change processes and targets, not just tools Measure use and outcomes, not licences Consult employee representatives early where law or agreements require it Say plainly what happens to time saved: more capacity for growth, better service, reskilling into new roles, or slower hiring. Silence on this is the fastest way to lose trust and adoption. Key formulas Hours AI could free in a role F = Σ k h k · a k Weekly hours per task times a planning factor for that kind of work (routine 0.7, information 0.4, drafting 0.3, judgment 0.1, relationships 0). Replace the factors with pilot measurements. Routine hours Information hours Drafting hours Judgment hours Relationship hours = ≈ 7.9 hours / week Sources & review Concept page · included in the monthly review Primary references for the ideas on this page. Deep ML fundamentals → New to me Learning Confident Bias–variance trade-off Intermediate Simple models underfit (high bias); flexible models overfit (high variance). Good models balance the two.
